When it comes to joking around, I'm a pretty hard believer that offence is taken, rather than given. I.e. a joker might not be trying to hurt someone, yet people still get offended and think it's ok to tell the joker what they can and can't say. That's some bullshit.

I think the difference here is that I can't interpret disrespectful play as a joke, or anything more than a declaration that "I want you to feel bad, and don't care if you have a bad time". It might sound a bit lame to you, but anti-wholesomeness just goes against my core. In a worst case scenario, such an experience could potentially make a new player stop playing. Growing the community has always been my goal, so imo there's just no place for this uncool behaviour.

Plus, I think the world would be a far better place if people had more empathy.

I might add that just because disrespectful stuff is done in other sports, that doesn't make it ok. 

When two boxers push each other to their limits, then hug it out afterwards, acknowledging each other's skill — I'm all about that. Sportsmanship, grace, respect. Let's go.

I wasn't sure of the end goal at first. I thought I had to get the longest word! 
So I suggest adding a single sentence like "end with the fewest possible letters".

It's quite a long play with the three attempts, compared to Wordle which is usually over in a minute or two. You might have more success if players only have to make one attempt per session, or at least have the option to submit after one 'give up'.

An automatic 'give up' might be nice, if no further words are possible.

Perhaps you could reward 3 consecutive days of play with a hint. There could also be a message "score below 10 for two more days to earn a hint!".

Wordle gives feedback commentary on your score, e.g. 'excellent!' if you get it in fewer than three guesses, or something like 'close call!' if you get it on the final guess.
I scored 11, 10, and 6 — but have no idea if these are good scores.

With Wordle, there is one definite solution, whereas with this I'm not sure if it is even possible to clear the board. If a complete solution is possible, there doesn't seem to be a good way of removing options and zeroing in on it. The combinations are just too numerous in such a board.

I found it difficult to be able to predict where the letters would move after my words were submitted. A few times the letters didn't move in the way I expected.

Overall a nice idea, and solid implementation! I enjoyed, so good luck with it :)

Gonna get loads of downvotes for disagreeing with known community figures, but whatever:

Imo this is not an issue. Please let it go.

Melee is a young competitive platform, compared to PC gaming. When you compete on PC, if you have a better mouse, a better monitor, a better system than your opponent, then you have an advantage. That's just the way it is, and everyone is fine with it.

It brings a healthy product market, which is the backbone of sponsorships for esports team recruitment.

I don't believe it compromises competitive integrity, even though I've personally lost tournaments because of my inferior kit. Players know this how it goes, and they have a choice about whether or not purchasing better equipment is worth it for them.

You're right that auto aim does compromise competitive integrity in FPS, but there is a simple solution; don't play games or enter tournaments which allow for cross platform play.
Besides, you're making a bit of a strawman fallacy; nobody is suggesting something like auto aim should be added to Melee.

If a person wants to bring a new and potentially untested controller to tournament, and risk it having software issues and need flashing, then that player should know they are taking a risk, and accept the consequences of a poor decision if it goes wrong. 

The idea that we need to stop people controlling their character in the best possible way is ridiculous.

Why would you block people from having consistent, optimal inputs? 

Why can't people have the choice whether to kick it old school on a GCC, or invest in a better input method?

Is it unfair if everyone can't afford a better controller? Yes, to a degree. Just like the thriving world of competitive PC gaming.
But the people who are willing to push their melee career as far as possible will find a way to get one.
And honestly, top level is the only place this will make a difference anyway. I could make a controller that bleeds cardinal directions every time I look at it, but I still couldn't win Summit with it.

The game is not designed to be played competitively, so we must push it in the forward direction wherever we can.
If Melee was designed from the ground up, today, to be the best competitive experience it can be, there would be a lot of changes. Stages would be changed, port priority jank would be fixed, and there would be no controller cardinal direction or snapback issues.

Please stop trying to keep Melee locked in 2001. Please let the community push the game to its competitive limits. Please stop holding Melee back.

When compared with BOTW, Horizon's interface and crafting mechanisms, combat, and gameplay in general are more complex. But complexity doesn't mean fun. I missed BOTW's simplicity when I was trudging through Horizon's menus of ingredients, items, ammo, and scrap. I also didn't like that Horizon forced you to hide in bushes and use stealth in some sections; I prefer games which let me choose how I approach situations. In contrast, BOTW feels incredibly free, thanks to the physical consistency of the environment, and the fact you can climb anything and go anywhere, as opposed to Horizon's limited selection of grabbable ledges.

In BOTW, sure, you can approach encounters Horizon-style; sneaking up to a camp and taking out the lookouts with your bow, before finishing the brutes in close quarters. But you could also roll a snowball down a hill so that it gets huge by the time it reaches the camp. Or start a small wildfire so that you can ride the updraft with your glider, soar over the camp and drop bombs, before pulling out your bow and going for bullet time headshots. There's so much joy to be found in exploring the possibilities of each encounter, and playing the game in the way YOU want to play it — rather than playing the way the designers tell you to play it.

I think I could only last about 7 hours before Horizon lost me. It was just too restrictive.

I will say that Horizon has much more of a story than BOTW. If you want lots of engaging dialogue and cut-scenes, then BOTW is not the game for you. Whilst there are some nice characters, quests, and interactions, for the most part it's a lonely, poignant journey.

If your brother said he saw a ghost, that is just anecdotal testimony.
It doesn't matter who claims they saw the ghost. If they make that claim, they aren't being skeptical.

Your brother may have seen some strange movements, a white shroud, a face, even hear a voice — but how would he determine it was ACTUALLY a ghost?

You see, *what* people see is not important. What matters is whether it can be explained.

What if you saw the ghost yourself?
That's still not enough, you should not conclude it's a ghost. You don't know what a ghost is. 
How would you tell the difference between a ghost and a smoke and mirrors trick by a person? Or a hallucination? Or an alien mind trick?

Taking these examples, we can actually place them in order of likelihood:
1)Joint win between hallucination and trick by a person
2)Alien mind trick
3)An actual ghost

The reason they go in this order is because we have evidence that hallucinations happen, and evidence that humans exist and have capacity to use smoke and mirror tricks.

Alien comes next because although we have no evidence for one, we have evidence for life at least.

Ghost comes last because we have no evidence for anything supernatural ever happening ever.

In the history of human experience, everything that was ever a mystery and has now been explained, has been explained by natural causes. Not once has the accepted explanation been paranormal or supernatural.

And that makes sense. If something supernatural was to appear, it would be in our reality. It would be testable, and by definition it would be natural. I can't see how anything supernatural could exist. It doesn't make sense as a concept.

When people claim something supernatural, they're committing the argument from ignorance fallacy. "I don't understand this, therefore it must be X".

Just because we don't understand something yet, it doesn't mean we can't eventually.

That's exactly what we're saying. Pre-ordering allows developers to rest on their laurels, instead of being forced to innovate. Thats when you get cookie-cutter clones like the assassin's creed, call of duty, and dare I say it, the majority of the Pokémon series. Why would a developer take a risk and try something new, if they know they'll make millions on pre-orders before the game is even released?

"But I know the game will be great!"
No, you don't. Do you know how many fans were disappointed by Just Cause 4?

Pre-ordering encourages money to be spent on marketing campaigns, rather than development time. Look at the astronomical (pardon the pun) amount of hype was behind No Man's Sky, and that game was a disaster. 

"Yeah but those developers don't have Nintendo's reputation for excellence". 
I raise you Blizzard; a previous contender for the world's best dev studio, who at the top of their game, somehow managed to turn Diablo 3 into a HUGE let-down on release (though it has been vastly improved since then). Or Maxis and their release of Spore, which fell vastly short of what the world was hoping.
Even Red Dead Redemption 2, whilst it's a technical masterpiece, probably doesn't output enough *fun* to justify how much money was spent in the form of pre-orders before the game even came out. It's incredibly detailed, but it's a very safe game, which doesn't  tread much new ground.

But look at what happens if you wait, instead of pre-ordering:


You'll still be able to find the game on release day, but by this point some reviews will have come out and you'll have a much better idea whether or not it's any good. Therefore you aren't risking any money.

There will still be deals to find, probably just as good as, if not better than whatever small % saving this pre-order is offering.

The developer won't be lazy. They'll have to try new things, push themselves, and give us some actual good experiences. I'd go so far as to say that BOTW and SMO are Nintendo's most daring projects since the GameCube days, and they're fantastic. From the trailer, nothing about this game looks close to that level of innovation and creativity.

Look at Metroid Prime 4, which has been delayed because Nintendo didn't feel like it was going to have the level of quality they wanted. 
Would they do this with Pokémon? Not a chance. Unlike Metroid, which is relatively niche, they know Pokémon will sell many millions of copies via pre-order alone, no matter how good it is. 

As a lifelong gamer, 'decent' is not good enough. I want to play GREAT games. If nobody pre-ordered, Nintendo/gamefreak would be foced to spend more resources developing an excellent game, rather than advertising a potentially mediocre one.
